An operating system is the software layer that makes a computer useful. In this section, you'll install Linux on classroom computers, learn your way around the desktop and terminal, inspect the hardware, and begin troubleshooting networks and software.

## Learning path

::: {.ter-path-grid}
::: {.ter-path-card}
### 1. Choose a distribution

Compare Linux distributions and choose one that fits the computer and the job.

[Open the distribution guide](choosing-a-distribution.qmd)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### 2. Install and commission Linux

Prepare the computer, confirm the correct drive, install Linux Mint, create accounts, update it, and check that the hardware works.

[Open the Linux Mint installation guide](install-linux-mint.qmd)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### 3. Use the terminal

Move through folders, create and edit files, read command help, and inspect running processes.

[Open Terminal Basics](terminal-basics.qmd)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### 4. Inspect the hardware

Use the desktop and commands to identify the CPU, memory, storage, operating system, and available sensors.

[Open Hardware Inventory](hardware-inventory.qmd)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### 5. Diagnose a network

Find the local address, gateway, and DNS settings. Use simple tests to locate a connection problem.

[Open Networking Diagnosis](networking-diagnosis.qmd)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### 6. Compare performance

Plan a fair test, record repeatable measurements, graph the results, and explain the limits of the evidence.

[Open Performance & Benchmarking](performance-benchmarking.qmd)
:::

::: {.ter-path-card}
### 7. Remote administration

Use SSH, file transfer, and tmux on a teacher-approved computer or isolated classroom network.

[Open SSH & Administration](ssh-administration.qmd)
:::
:::
